title: Polling vs Interrupts: How the CPU Talks to a Slow Disk
topic: Polling vs interrupts — polling spins the CPU on a device status register until the device is ready; an interrupt lets the CPU run other work and be woken when the device is done. For a slow device the difference is most of the CPU's time.

beats.narration: A disk read takes millions of CPU cycles. While the disk works, what should the processor do?

elements.content: The CPU is fast. The disk is slow. Who waits?

beats.narration: Polling means the CPU asks the device, again and again — is it ready yet? Every check is a wasted cycle, and almost every check returns no.

elements.content: Two horizontal bars: top labelled CPU, bottom labelled DISK
CPU bar fills left to right with red 'check?' segments until the disk indicates ready
DISK bar shows one long busy segment ending at the same point
almost every poll returns no — the CPU did no useful work

beats.narration: Interrupts flip the question around. The CPU issues the request, runs something else, and the device fires an interrupt when it is done.

elements.content: Same two bars: CPU now fills with green 'other work' segments while DISK is busy
When DISK finishes, an interrupt arrow drops down onto the CPU bar
CPU bar shows a short amber 'handler' segment immediately after the interrupt

beats.narration: Stack the two side by side. With polling the CPU's wait is wasted. With interrupts that same time becomes throughput for the rest of the system.

elements.content: Top mini-bar: polling CPU — almost entirely red
Bottom mini-bar: interrupt CPU — green for most of the wait, a thin amber handler at the end
same wall-clock — very different CPU utilisation

beats.narration: Interrupts give you concurrency for free. Polling only makes sense when the wait is so short an interrupt would cost more than the wait itself.

elements.content: poll only when the device is faster than an interrupt is cheap
